title: Predictably Unpredictable
author: Mr. Nickhart
summary: Mr. Nickhart examines the paradox at the heart of school improvement: schools are complex adaptive systems whose outcomes are unpredictable, yet experienced leaders navigate them partly through pattern recognition. He argues that improvement plans are necessarily written as if cause-and-effect are direct, but that this is a presentation convention, not a description of reality. The real problem arises when leaders begin to believe the neat narrative of their own plans. Drawing on systems thinking principles -- cause and effect are not closely related in time and space; the harder you push, the harder the system pushes back; easy fixes tend to loop back in -- he calls for better pattern recognition in school leaders rather than better plan templates. The article closes by framing June's Leadership Handbook post as an attempt to provide that practical pattern-recognition scaffolding.
points: Complex systems are unpredictable in their outcomes but can have predictable emergent patterns of behaviour -- learning to recognise those patterns (push harder ? pushback; new initiative ? early promise then cultural absorption; address one issue ? another emerges) is the real skill of school improvement leadership.

Improvement plans must present a linear story for governance and accountability, but treating that story as a causal description of reality is the category error that causes leaders to look first at implementation fidelity when plans fail, rather than at the system dynamics underneath.

Resistance to a mandated change is often not resistance for the sake of it but rational adaptation by people responding to the pressures and information available to them -- compliance rises, risk-taking falls, the system stabilises itself.
The same action will not have the same effect everywhere; Ashby's law of requisite variety implies that a single tightly defined approach cannot absorb the complexity of a varied system.

Because cause and effect are not closely related in time and space, improvements may only become visible in headline measures months after the underlying change has taken hold -- early-warning signals (trust, learning time, attention) matter more than waiting for the data.
quotes: Schools are complex, as opposed to complicated. We can argue that schools are complex, adaptive systems which goes hand in hand with rejecting the notion that most of what we do is merely complicated.
We design plans based on how we hope the system behaves, not how it actually behaves.
The plan helps us explain improvement but it does not necessarily cause it.

One is that the harder you push, the harder the system pushes back. Increased pressure often produces behaviours that appear to align with expectations but do not necessarily reflect deeper change. Compliance rises and risk taking falls.
What looks like resistance can be adaptation. And adaptation is exactly what complex systems do.

We need better school improvement pattern recognition. We're already good at the structures and templates for narrating improvement but we need to proverbially sharpen our axe; sharpen our conception of how it is that (our) schools improve and plan for emergence.
